studies.opening: Row 2 has 4 printed symbols; column A has 2. Compare their remaining sun and moon quotas with the no-three rule before extending either line.
studies.structuralDistinction: Row 2 has 4 printed symbols; column A has 2. The asymmetry between a more-clued row and a lightly marked crossing column shapes this board's opening.
intendedReasoningPath: Row 2 has 4 printed symbols; column A has 2. Start with equal line totals and no three identical neighbors, checking both axes at every shared cell.
Compare the balanced line patterns allowed by each row with the crossing column marks, then carry each exclusion into its perpendicular line.
Before accepting a completed line, check that it differs from every other row or column on that axis; local legality is not enough.
studies.temptingMistake: A row pattern can satisfy its own balance and triple rules while making the crossing column impossible or duplicating another complete line.

studies.opening: Begin where E2 < F2 meets E1 > E2; keep the shared rank inside both comparison bounds while respecting the row and column sets.
studies.structuralDistinction: This 7×7 Latin square has 19 horizontal and 13 vertical inequalities; E2 < F2 and E1 > E2 meet at E2.
intendedReasoningPath: Start at the crossing E2 < F2 and E1 > E2. Translate adjacent comparisons into ranges, then carry those bounds through their connected chains.
Remove ranks already used in the same row and column, and revisit each incident comparison whenever a neighboring value is placed.
Use the perpendicular bounds together before settling a rank; a value available in one line can still violate an inequality or its crossing line.
studies.temptingMistake: Checking a rank against its row and column alone overlooks the comparison at the crossing and can leave a locally plausible but impossible value.
